1	---
2	title: "Getting started with RaCInG"
3	output:
4	  rmarkdown::html_vignette:
5	    toc: true
6	    number_sections: false
7	vignette: >
8	  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Getting started with RaCInG}
9	  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
10	  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
11	---
12	
13	```{r, include = FALSE}
14	knitr::opts_chunk$set(
15	  collapse = TRUE,
16	  comment = "#>",
17	  fig.width = 7,
18	  fig.height = 4
19	)
20	```
21	
22	## Overview
23	
24	`RaCInG` reconstructs patient-specific cell-cell communication networks from bulk
25	RNA-seq data. The package supports two complementary workflows:
26	
27	- a **kernel-based** approach for fast deterministic feature extraction, and
28	- a **Monte Carlo** approach for simulation-based network summaries.
29	
30	This vignette shows the recommended workflow and the most important entry points for
31	new users, using both the bundled, ready-made example data and a real bulk RNA-seq
32	counts matrix run through the full preprocessing pipeline.
33	
34	## Installation
35	
36	### Install from GitHub
37	
38	```{r eval = FALSE}
39	# install.packages("remotes")
40	remotes::install_github("VeraPancaldiLab/RaCInG_package")
41	library(RaCInG)
42	```
43	
44	### Install from a local checkout
45	
46	```{r eval = FALSE}
47	# install.packages("devtools")
48	devtools::install(".")
49	library(RaCInG)
50	```
51	
52	If you want to build the RaCInG input matrices directly from raw counts, install the
53	optional preprocessing dependencies used by `prepare_input_files()`:
54	
55	```{r eval = FALSE}
56	install.packages(c("ggplot2", "nnls"))
57	# ADImpute and OmnipathR are available from Bioconductor:
58	BiocManager::install(c("ADImpute", "OmnipathR"))
59	# liana and multideconv are GitHub-only:
60	remotes::install_github(c("saezlab/liana", "VeraPancaldiLab/multideconv"))
61	```
62	
63	## Workflow at a glance
64	
65	| Goal | Function | Output |
66	| --- | --- | --- |
67	| Build input matrices from raw counts | `prepare_input_files()` | Named list with `L`, `R`, `C`, `LR` matrices and labels |
68	| Compute deterministic features | `compute_racing_kernel()` | Kernel arrays + feature matrix |
69	| Compute simulation summaries | `compute_racing_montecarlo()` | Processed Monte Carlo results |
70	| Decompose a score into ligand-receptor pairs | `computeLRContributions()` / `computeWedgeLRContributions()` / `computeTriangleLRContributions()` + `plotLRContributions()` | Ranked contributions and a LIANA-style dot plot |
71	| Compare clinical groups | `wilcox_group_test()` + `top_features_plot()` | Statistics table and ranked bar plot |
72	| Relate features to a continuous score | `correlate_features_with_score()` + `correlation_plot()` | Correlation table and rainfall plot |
73	
74	## How `prepare_input_files()` builds its inputs
75	
76	Starting from a raw gene-by-sample counts matrix, `prepare_input_files()` chains
77	together several packages so you never have to run them by hand:
78	
79	1. **Normalization**: counts are converted to TPM with `ADImpute::NormalizeTPM()`.
80	2. **Deconvolution**: cell-type fractions are estimated with
81	   `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()` (defaults to the Quantiseq method, but
82	   any method(s) supported by multideconv can be passed via `deconv_method`).
83	3. **Subgroup analysis**: `multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis()` identifies
84	   groups of highly correlated deconvolution features (e.g. several methods agreeing
85	   on the same cell type) and collapses them into a single column per resolved cell
86	   type, discarding low-quality/high-zero features along the way. Column names are
87	   then standardized and stripped of any method/signature prefix, giving short,
88	   consistent cell-type labels (e.g. `"B.cells"`, `"CD4.regulatory"`).
89	4. **Cell-type expression profiles**: for every gene, a non-negative least squares
90	   fit of bulk expression against the cell-type fractions gives one expression value
91	   per gene per resolved cell type.
92	5. **Ligand-receptor prior knowledge**: a curated, OmniPath-backed consensus network
93	   is retrieved with `liana::get_curated_omni()` and restricted to ligand/receptor
94	   roles, then decomplexified into single-gene subunits.
95	6. **Filtering and assembly**: ligand-receptor pairs are kept only where both genes
96	   are expressed above 10 TPM in the relevant cell types, and the `Lmatrix`,
97	   `Rmatrix`, `Cmatrix`, and `LRmatrix` inputs (see below) are assembled and written
98	   to `output_folder`.
99	
100	You can skip any of steps 2-5 by supplying your own `deconv`, `cell_expr_profile`,
101	or `cc_network` directly.
102	
103	## Recommended workflow with a real bulk RNA-seq dataset
104	
105	The examples below use the raw bulk RNA-seq counts matrix bundled with the
106	`multideconv` package (`raw_counts`, from Mariathasan et al. 2018, a
107	urothelial/bladder cancer cohort profiled for anti-PD-L1 response) to exercise the
108	full pipeline end to end, from raw counts to features to statistics. These chunks
109	call out to the network (OmniPath/LIANA) and run real deconvolution, so they are
110	shown but not evaluated when the vignette is built; run them interactively to try
111	the full pipeline yourself.
112	
113	### 1. Build input matrices from raw counts
114	
115	```{r eval = FALSE}
116	data(raw_counts, package = "multideconv")
117	counts_matrix <- as.matrix(raw_counts)
118	
119	input <- prepare_input_files(
120	  counts = counts_matrix,
121	  output_folder = "Results/",
122	  file_name = "mariathasan",
123	  deconv_method = "Quantiseq"
124	)
125	
126	str(input, max.level = 1)
127	input$celltypes
128	```
129	
130	### 2. Run the kernel method
131	
132	The kernel method is the fastest way to derive direct, wedge, triangle, or GSCC
133	features across patients.
134	You can pass `counts` to let the function compute inputs
135	automatically, or supply previously computed matrices via `input_data`.
136	
137	```{r eval = FALSE}
138	# Option A: from raw counts (runs prepare_input_files internally)
139	kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
140	  counts = counts_matrix,
141	  output_folder = tempdir(),
142	  file_name = "mariathasan",
143	  communication_type = "W",
144	  norm = TRUE
145	)
146	
147	# Option B: from pre-computed input matrices (skips preprocessing)
148	kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
149	  input_data = input,
150	  communication_type = "W",
151	  norm = TRUE
152	)
153	
154	head(kernel_res$features[, 1:5])
155	```
156	
157	Feature columns with no possible ligand-receptor pathway in any patient (structurally
158	zero for every patient) are dropped automatically, rather than returned as dead
159	all-zero columns -- so `ncol(kernel_res$features)` is usually well below the full
160	combinatorial count of cell-type combinations.
161	
162	`communication_type` also accepts a vector, e.g. `c("D", "W", "TT", "GSCC")`. The
163	kernel itself (the expensive analytic step) is only ever computed once regardless of
164	how many types you request, so if you want more than one feature family there is no
165	need to call `compute_racing_kernel()` again -- request them all in one call instead:
166	
167	```{r eval = FALSE}
168	kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
169	  input_data = input,
170	  communication_type = c("D", "W", "TT", "GSCC"),
171	  norm = TRUE
172	)
173	
174	# features is now a named list, one data frame per requested type
175	names(kernel_res$features)
176	head(kernel_res$features$D[, 1:5])
177	```
178	
179	### 3. Run the Monte Carlo method
180	
181	Use the Monte Carlo workflow when you want simulation-based summaries or uncertainty
182	estimates from repeated graph realizations. The same `input_data` shortcut is
183	available here. Simulation cost scales with `Ncells` and `Ngraphs`; the values below
184	are kept small for a quick illustration.
185	
186	```{r eval = FALSE}
187	set.seed(1)
188	mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
189	  counts = counts_matrix,
190	  output_folder = tempdir(),
191	  deconv_method = "Quantiseq",
192	  file_name = "mariathasan",
193	  nPatients = 3,
194	  communication_type = "W",
195	  Ncells = 100,
196	  Ngraphs = 10,
197	  Ndegree = 3,
198	  norm = TRUE
199	)
200	
201	# Or from pre-computed inputs:
202	mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
203	  input_data = input,
204	  output_folder = tempdir(),
205	  file_name = "mariathasan",
206	  communication_type = "W",
207	  Ncells = 100,
208	  Ngraphs = 10,
209	  Ndegree = 3,
210	  norm = TRUE
211	)
212	
213	head(mc_res$output$mean[, 1:5])
214	```
215	
216	As with the kernel method, `communication_type` accepts a vector (any combination of
217	`"D"`, `"W"`, `"TT"`, `"CT"`, `"GSCC"`). Every requested type is extracted from the
218	*same* simulated graphs, instead of re-simulating a fresh set of graphs per type --
219	graph generation, not feature extraction, is the expensive part of a Monte Carlo run:
220	
221	```{r eval = FALSE}
222	mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
223	  input_data = input,
224	  communication_type = c("D", "W", "TT", "CT", "GSCC"),
225	  Ncells = 100,
226	  Ngraphs = 10,
227	  Ndegree = 3,
228	  norm = TRUE,
229	  output_folder = tempdir(),
230	  file_name = "mariathasan"
231	)
232	
233	# output is now a named list, one entry per requested type
234	names(mc_res$output)
235	head(mc_res$output$D$mean[, 1:5])
236	```
237	
238	Patients are independent of each other, so larger runs can be parallelized across
239	cores with `ncores` (via `parallel`/`doParallel`/`foreach`, so it works the same way
240	on Windows, macOS, and Linux):
241	
242	```{r eval = FALSE}
243	mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
244	  input_data = input,
245	  communication_type = "D",
246	  Ncells = 500,
247	  Ngraphs = 100,
248	  Ndegree = 20,
249	  ncores = 4,
250	  output_folder = tempdir(),
251	  file_name = "mariathasan"
252	)
253	```
254	
255	### 4. Compare clinical groups
256	
257	Once features are available in a patient-by-feature matrix, use the built-in Wilcoxon
258	workflow to compare groups. `wilcox_group_test()` reports, per feature and per pair
259	of groups, the Wilcoxon statistic, fold change, and (jointly) FDR-adjusted p-value;
260	`top_features_plot()` shows the top up/down features by `log2(fold change)` as a
261	ranked bar chart.
262	
263	```{r eval = FALSE}
264	grouping <- c("Responder", "Responder", "Non-responder", "Non-responder")
265	wilcox_results <- wilcox_group_test(kernel_res$features, grouping)
266	head(wilcox_results)
267	top_features_plot(wilcox_results, top_n = 15)
268	```
269	
270	With more than two groups, every pairwise comparison is run automatically; subset
271	`wilcox_results` by `Comparison` (or pass a two-group subset to `top_features_plot()`) to
272	inspect one pair at a time.
273	
274	### 5. Correlate features with a continuous score
275	
276	If you have a continuous per-patient score (e.g. an immune response or survival
277	score), `correlate_features_with_score()` reports the Spearman correlation between
278	every feature and the score, pooled across all patients and, optionally, within
279	groups. `correlation_plot()` shows the top positive and negative correlations.
280	
281	```{r eval = FALSE}
282	response_score <- setNames(rnorm(nrow(kernel_res$features)), rownames(kernel_res$features))
283	corr_results <- correlate_features_with_score(kernel_res$features, response_score)
284	head(corr_results)
285	correlation_plot(corr_results, top_n = 10)
286	```
287	
288	## Notes
289	
290	- `compute_racing_kernel()` and `compute_racing_montecarlo()` are the main entry points.
291	- Both accept an `input_data` argument with pre-computed matrices (as returned by
292	  `prepare_input_files()`), which skips all preprocessing.
293	- `prepare_input_files()` requires the optional packages listed under Installation
294	  for deconvolution and prior-network assembly.
295	- The original Python implementation is available at
296	  <https://github.com/SysBioOncology/RaCInG>.
297	
298	## Understanding the input files
299	
300	RaCInG requires four matrices and associated label vectors that describe the
301	cell-cell communication landscape for a cohort of patients. The table below
302	summarises each component:
303	
304	| Component | Dimensions | Description |
305	| --- | --- | --- |
306	| **Lmatrix** | cell types × ligands | Binary compatibility matrix: `1` if that ligand is expressed above `expr_threshold` in that cell type, `0` otherwise. Rows are cell types; columns are ligands. |
307	| **Rmatrix** | cell types × receptors | Binary compatibility matrix: `1` if that receptor is expressed above `expr_threshold` in that cell type, `0` otherwise. Same row order as `Lmatrix`. |
308	| **Cmatrix** | patients × cell types | Cell-type fraction for each patient. Each row sums to 1. |
309	| **LRmatrix** | ligands × receptors × patients | 3-D tensor of ligand–receptor interaction weights. Each patient slice is normalised to sum to 1. |
310	| **celltypes** | character vector | Alphabetically sorted cell-type names (shared across L, R, and C). |
311	| **ligands** | character vector | Ligand names matching the columns of `Lmatrix` and the first axis of `LRmatrix`. |
312	| **receptors** | character vector | Receptor names matching the columns of `Rmatrix` and the second axis of `LRmatrix`. |
313	| **Sign_matrix** | ligands × receptors | Optional matrix encoding known stimulatory (+1) or inhibitory (−1) interactions. Zeros indicate unknown. |
314	
315	These inputs are typically generated by `prepare_input_files()` from a raw
316	counts matrix, or they can be assembled manually from pre-existing deconvolution
317	and prior-network data. The bundled `skcm_example` dataset provides a ready-made
318	example of this structure.
319	
320	### Inspecting the example inputs
321	
322	```{r}
323	library(RaCInG)
324	data(skcm_example)
325	
326	# Overall structure
327	str(skcm_example, max.level = 1)
328	```
329	
330	```{r}
331	# Lmatrix: 9 cell types × 276 ligands
332	dim(skcm_example$Lmatrix)
333	skcm_example$Lmatrix[1:4, 1:5]
334	```
335	
336	```{r}
337	# Rmatrix: 9 cell types × 298 receptors
338	dim(skcm_example$Rmatrix)
339	skcm_example$Rmatrix[1:4, 1:5]
340	```
341	
342	```{r}
343	# Cmatrix: 10 patients × 9 cell types (rows sum to 1)
344	dim(skcm_example$Cmatrix)
345	skcm_example$Cmatrix[1:4, ]
346	```
347	
348	```{r}
349	# LRmatrix: 276 ligands × 298 receptors × 10 patients (3-D tensor)
350	dim(skcm_example$LRmatrix)
351	# First patient slice, top-left corner:
352	skcm_example$LRmatrix[1:4, 1:4, 1]
353	```
354	
355	```{r}
356	# Label vectors
357	skcm_example$celltypes
358	head(skcm_example$ligands, 10)
359	head(skcm_example$receptors, 10)
360	```
361	
362	## Running with the bundled example data
363	
364	The `skcm_example` list shown above can be passed directly to the kernel or Monte
365	Carlo workflows via the `input_data` parameter, and to the statistical analysis
366	functions once features have been computed.
367	
368	### Kernel method on the example data
369	
370	```{r}
371	kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
372	  input_data   = skcm_example,
373	  output_folder = tempdir(),
374	  communication_type = "D",
375	  norm = TRUE
376	)
377	
378	head(kernel_res$features[, 1:5])
379	```
380	
381	### Decomposing a score into ligand-receptor pairs
382	
383	`compute_kernel()` sums over every ligand-receptor pair to produce one score per
384	cell-type pair, so that score alone can't tell you which ligand-receptor pairs drove
385	it. `computeLRContributions()` recovers that breakdown for one sender-receiver pair
386	(exploiting that the kernel formula is linear in `LRmatrix`, so each pair's
387	contribution can be computed directly and sums back exactly to the original score),
388	and `plotLRContributions()` shows the top contributors as a LIANA-style dot plot (dot
389	size = share of that pair's total score, color = raw contribution).
390	
391	```{r}
392	lr_contrib <- computeLRContributions(
393	  Lmatrix = skcm_example$Lmatrix, Rmatrix = skcm_example$Rmatrix,
394	  Cmatrix = skcm_example$Cmatrix, LRmatrix = skcm_example$LRmatrix,
395	  celltypes = skcm_example$celltypes, sender = "Tumor", receiver = "CD8+ T"
396	)
397	head(lr_contrib)
398	plotLRContributions(lr_contrib, top_n = 10)
399	```
400	
401	The same decomposition extends to Wedges (`computeWedgeLRContributions()`) and
402	Triangles (`computeTriangleLRContributions()`): since those motifs multiply their
403	edges together rather than sum them, each function instead decomposes every
404	individual edge of the motif separately (`PctOfTotal` is then relative to that edge's
405	own score, not the whole motif), which `plotLRContributions()` shows faceted by edge.
406	
407	### Statistical analysis on the example data

409	```{r}
410	set.seed(1)
411	grouping <- sample(c("GroupA", "GroupB"), nrow(kernel_res$features), replace = TRUE)
412	wilcox_results <- wilcox_group_test(kernel_res$features, grouping)
413	head(wilcox_results)
414	top_features_plot(wilcox_results, top_n = 10)
415	```
416	
417	```{r}
418	response_score <- setNames(rnorm(nrow(kernel_res$features)), rownames(kernel_res$features))
419	corr_results <- correlate_features_with_score(kernel_res$features, response_score)
420	head(corr_results)
421	correlation_plot(corr_results, top_n = 10)
422	```
423	
424	### Monte Carlo method on the example data
425

427	set.seed(42)
428	mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
429	  input_data   = skcm_example,

432	  nPatients     = 2,

---
title: "Getting started with RaCInG"
output:
  rmarkdown::html_vignette:
    toc: true
    number_sections: false
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Getting started with RaCInG}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4
)
```

## Overview

`RaCInG` reconstructs patient-specific cell-cell communication networks from bulk
RNA-seq data. The package supports two complementary workflows:

- a **kernel-based** approach for fast deterministic feature extraction, and
- a **Monte Carlo** approach for simulation-based network summaries.

This vignette shows the recommended workflow and the most important entry points for
new users, using both the bundled, ready-made example data and a real bulk RNA-seq
counts matrix run through the full preprocessing pipeline.

## Installation

### Install from GitHub

```{r eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("VeraPancaldiLab/RaCInG_package")
library(RaCInG)
```

### Install from a local checkout

```{r eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install(".")
library(RaCInG)
```

If you want to build the RaCInG input matrices directly from raw counts, install the
optional preprocessing dependencies used by `prepare_input_files()`:

```{r eval = FALSE}
install.packages(c("ggplot2", "nnls"))
# ADImpute and OmnipathR are available from Bioconductor:
BiocManager::install(c("ADImpute", "OmnipathR"))
# liana and multideconv are GitHub-only:
remotes::install_github(c("saezlab/liana", "VeraPancaldiLab/multideconv"))
```

## Workflow at a glance

| Goal | Function | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Build input matrices from raw counts | `prepare_input_files()` | Named list with `L`, `R`, `C`, `LR` matrices and labels |
| Compute deterministic features | `compute_racing_kernel()` | Kernel arrays + feature matrix |
| Compute simulation summaries | `compute_racing_montecarlo()` | Processed Monte Carlo results |
| Decompose a score into ligand-receptor pairs | `computeLRContributions()` / `computeWedgeLRContributions()` / `computeTriangleLRContributions()` + `plotLRContributions()` | Ranked contributions and a LIANA-style dot plot |
| Compare clinical groups | `wilcox_group_test()` + `top_features_plot()` | Statistics table and ranked bar plot |
| Relate features to a continuous score | `correlate_features_with_score()` + `correlation_plot()` | Correlation table and rainfall plot |

## How `prepare_input_files()` builds its inputs

Starting from a raw gene-by-sample counts matrix, `prepare_input_files()` chains
together several packages so you never have to run them by hand:

1. **Normalization**: counts are converted to TPM with `ADImpute::NormalizeTPM()`.
2. **Deconvolution**: cell-type fractions are estimated with
   `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()` (defaults to the Quantiseq method, but
   any method(s) supported by multideconv can be passed via `deconv_method`).
3. **Subgroup analysis**: `multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis()` identifies
   groups of highly correlated deconvolution features (e.g. several methods agreeing
   on the same cell type) and collapses them into a single column per resolved cell
   type, discarding low-quality/high-zero features along the way. Column names are
   then standardized and stripped of any method/signature prefix, giving short,
   consistent cell-type labels (e.g. `"B.cells"`, `"CD4.regulatory"`).
4. **Cell-type expression profiles**: for every gene, a non-negative least squares
   fit of bulk expression against the cell-type fractions gives one expression value
   per gene per resolved cell type.
5. **Ligand-receptor prior knowledge**: a curated, OmniPath-backed consensus network
   is retrieved with `liana::get_curated_omni()` and restricted to ligand/receptor
   roles, then decomplexified into single-gene subunits.
6. **Filtering and assembly**: ligand-receptor pairs are kept only where both genes
   are expressed above 10 TPM in the relevant cell types, and the `Lmatrix`,
   `Rmatrix`, `Cmatrix`, and `LRmatrix` inputs (see below) are assembled and written
   to `output_folder`.

You can skip any of steps 2-5 by supplying your own `deconv`, `cell_expr_profile`,
or `cc_network` directly.

## Recommended workflow with a real bulk RNA-seq dataset

The examples below use the raw bulk RNA-seq counts matrix bundled with the
`multideconv` package (`raw_counts`, from Mariathasan et al. 2018, a
urothelial/bladder cancer cohort profiled for anti-PD-L1 response) to exercise the
full pipeline end to end, from raw counts to features to statistics. These chunks
call out to the network (OmniPath/LIANA) and run real deconvolution, so they are
shown but not evaluated when the vignette is built; run them interactively to try
the full pipeline yourself.

### 1. Build input matrices from raw counts

```{r eval = FALSE}
data(raw_counts, package = "multideconv")
counts_matrix <- as.matrix(raw_counts)

input <- prepare_input_files(
  counts = counts_matrix,
  output_folder = "Results/",
  file_name = "mariathasan",
  deconv_method = "Quantiseq"
)

str(input, max.level = 1)
input$celltypes
```

### 2. Run the kernel method

The kernel method is the fastest way to derive direct, wedge, triangle, or GSCC
features across patients.
You can pass `counts` to let the function compute inputs
automatically, or supply previously computed matrices via `input_data`.

```{r eval = FALSE}
# Option A: from raw counts (runs prepare_input_files internally)
kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
  counts = counts_matrix,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  file_name = "mariathasan",
  communication_type = "W",
  norm = TRUE
)

# Option B: from pre-computed input matrices (skips preprocessing)
kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
  input_data = input,
  communication_type = "W",
  norm = TRUE
)

head(kernel_res$features[, 1:5])
```

Feature columns with no possible ligand-receptor pathway in any patient (structurally
zero for every patient) are dropped automatically, rather than returned as dead
all-zero columns -- so `ncol(kernel_res$features)` is usually well below the full
combinatorial count of cell-type combinations.

`communication_type` also accepts a vector, e.g. `c("D", "W", "TT", "GSCC")`. The
kernel itself (the expensive analytic step) is only ever computed once regardless of
how many types you request, so if you want more than one feature family there is no
need to call `compute_racing_kernel()` again -- request them all in one call instead:

```{r eval = FALSE}
kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
  input_data = input,
  communication_type = c("D", "W", "TT", "GSCC"),
  norm = TRUE
)

# features is now a named list, one data frame per requested type
names(kernel_res$features)
head(kernel_res$features$D[, 1:5])
```

### 3. Run the Monte Carlo method

Use the Monte Carlo workflow when you want simulation-based summaries or uncertainty
estimates from repeated graph realizations. The same `input_data` shortcut is
available here. Simulation cost scales with `Ncells` and `Ngraphs`; the values below
are kept small for a quick illustration.

```{r eval = FALSE}
set.seed(1)
mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
  counts = counts_matrix,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  deconv_method = "Quantiseq",
  file_name = "mariathasan",
  nPatients = 3,
  communication_type = "W",
  Ncells = 100,
  Ngraphs = 10,
  Ndegree = 3,
  norm = TRUE
)

# Or from pre-computed inputs:
mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
  input_data = input,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  file_name = "mariathasan",
  communication_type = "W",
  Ncells = 100,
  Ngraphs = 10,
  Ndegree = 3,
  norm = TRUE
)

head(mc_res$output$mean[, 1:5])
```

As with the kernel method, `communication_type` accepts a vector (any combination of
`"D"`, `"W"`, `"TT"`, `"CT"`, `"GSCC"`). Every requested type is extracted from the
*same* simulated graphs, instead of re-simulating a fresh set of graphs per type --
graph generation, not feature extraction, is the expensive part of a Monte Carlo run:

```{r eval = FALSE}
mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
  input_data = input,
  communication_type = c("D", "W", "TT", "CT", "GSCC"),
  Ncells = 100,
  Ngraphs = 10,
  Ndegree = 3,
  norm = TRUE,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  file_name = "mariathasan"
)

# output is now a named list, one entry per requested type
names(mc_res$output)
head(mc_res$output$D$mean[, 1:5])
```

Patients are independent of each other, so larger runs can be parallelized across
cores with `ncores` (via `parallel`/`doParallel`/`foreach`, so it works the same way
on Windows, macOS, and Linux):

```{r eval = FALSE}
mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
  input_data = input,
  communication_type = "D",
  Ncells = 500,
  Ngraphs = 100,
  Ndegree = 20,
  ncores = 4,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  file_name = "mariathasan"
)
```

### 4. Compare clinical groups

Once features are available in a patient-by-feature matrix, use the built-in Wilcoxon
workflow to compare groups. `wilcox_group_test()` reports, per feature and per pair
of groups, the Wilcoxon statistic, fold change, and (jointly) FDR-adjusted p-value;
`top_features_plot()` shows the top up/down features by `log2(fold change)` as a
ranked bar chart.

```{r eval = FALSE}
grouping <- c("Responder", "Responder", "Non-responder", "Non-responder")
wilcox_results <- wilcox_group_test(kernel_res$features, grouping)
head(wilcox_results)
top_features_plot(wilcox_results, top_n = 15)
```

With more than two groups, every pairwise comparison is run automatically; subset
`wilcox_results` by `Comparison` (or pass a two-group subset to `top_features_plot()`) to
inspect one pair at a time.

### 5. Correlate features with a continuous score

If you have a continuous per-patient score (e.g. an immune response or survival
score), `correlate_features_with_score()` reports the Spearman correlation between
every feature and the score, pooled across all patients and, optionally, within
groups. `correlation_plot()` shows the top positive and negative correlations.

```{r eval = FALSE}
response_score <- setNames(rnorm(nrow(kernel_res$features)), rownames(kernel_res$features))
corr_results <- correlate_features_with_score(kernel_res$features, response_score)
head(corr_results)
correlation_plot(corr_results, top_n = 10)
```

## Notes

- `compute_racing_kernel()` and `compute_racing_montecarlo()` are the main entry points.
- Both accept an `input_data` argument with pre-computed matrices (as returned by
  `prepare_input_files()`), which skips all preprocessing.
- `prepare_input_files()` requires the optional packages listed under Installation
  for deconvolution and prior-network assembly.
- The original Python implementation is available at
  <https://github.com/SysBioOncology/RaCInG>.

## Understanding the input files

RaCInG requires four matrices and associated label vectors that describe the
cell-cell communication landscape for a cohort of patients. The table below
summarises each component:

| Component | Dimensions | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Lmatrix** | cell types × ligands | Binary compatibility matrix: `1` if that ligand is expressed above `expr_threshold` in that cell type, `0` otherwise. Rows are cell types; columns are ligands. |
| **Rmatrix** | cell types × receptors | Binary compatibility matrix: `1` if that receptor is expressed above `expr_threshold` in that cell type, `0` otherwise. Same row order as `Lmatrix`. |
| **Cmatrix** | patients × cell types | Cell-type fraction for each patient. Each row sums to 1. |
| **LRmatrix** | ligands × receptors × patients | 3-D tensor of ligand–receptor interaction weights. Each patient slice is normalised to sum to 1. |
| **celltypes** | character vector | Alphabetically sorted cell-type names (shared across L, R, and C). |
| **ligands** | character vector | Ligand names matching the columns of `Lmatrix` and the first axis of `LRmatrix`. |
| **receptors** | character vector | Receptor names matching the columns of `Rmatrix` and the second axis of `LRmatrix`. |
| **Sign_matrix** | ligands × receptors | Optional matrix encoding known stimulatory (+1) or inhibitory (−1) interactions. Zeros indicate unknown. |

These inputs are typically generated by `prepare_input_files()` from a raw
counts matrix, or they can be assembled manually from pre-existing deconvolution
and prior-network data. The bundled `skcm_example` dataset provides a ready-made
example of this structure.

### Inspecting the example inputs

```{r}
library(RaCInG)
data(skcm_example)

# Overall structure
str(skcm_example, max.level = 1)
```

```{r}
# Lmatrix: 9 cell types × 276 ligands
dim(skcm_example$Lmatrix)
skcm_example$Lmatrix[1:4, 1:5]
```

```{r}
# Rmatrix: 9 cell types × 298 receptors
dim(skcm_example$Rmatrix)
skcm_example$Rmatrix[1:4, 1:5]
```

```{r}
# Cmatrix: 10 patients × 9 cell types (rows sum to 1)
dim(skcm_example$Cmatrix)
skcm_example$Cmatrix[1:4, ]
```

```{r}
# LRmatrix: 276 ligands × 298 receptors × 10 patients (3-D tensor)
dim(skcm_example$LRmatrix)
# First patient slice, top-left corner:
skcm_example$LRmatrix[1:4, 1:4, 1]
```

```{r}
# Label vectors
skcm_example$celltypes
head(skcm_example$ligands, 10)
head(skcm_example$receptors, 10)
```

## Running with the bundled example data

The `skcm_example` list shown above can be passed directly to the kernel or Monte
Carlo workflows via the `input_data` parameter, and to the statistical analysis
functions once features have been computed.

### Kernel method on the example data

```{r}
kernel_res <- compute_racing_kernel(
  input_data   = skcm_example,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  communication_type = "D",
  norm = TRUE
)

head(kernel_res$features[, 1:5])
```

### Decomposing a score into ligand-receptor pairs

`compute_kernel()` sums over every ligand-receptor pair to produce one score per
cell-type pair, so that score alone can't tell you which ligand-receptor pairs drove
it. `computeLRContributions()` recovers that breakdown for one sender-receiver pair
(exploiting that the kernel formula is linear in `LRmatrix`, so each pair's
contribution can be computed directly and sums back exactly to the original score),
and `plotLRContributions()` shows the top contributors as a LIANA-style dot plot (dot
size = share of that pair's total score, color = raw contribution).

```{r}
lr_contrib <- computeLRContributions(
  Lmatrix = skcm_example$Lmatrix, Rmatrix = skcm_example$Rmatrix,
  Cmatrix = skcm_example$Cmatrix, LRmatrix = skcm_example$LRmatrix,
  celltypes = skcm_example$celltypes, sender = "Tumor", receiver = "CD8+ T"
)
head(lr_contrib)
plotLRContributions(lr_contrib, top_n = 10)
```

The same decomposition extends to Wedges (`computeWedgeLRContributions()`) and
Triangles (`computeTriangleLRContributions()`): since those motifs multiply their
edges together rather than sum them, each function instead decomposes every
individual edge of the motif separately (`PctOfTotal` is then relative to that edge's
own score, not the whole motif), which `plotLRContributions()` shows faceted by edge.

### Statistical analysis on the example data

```{r}
set.seed(1)
grouping <- sample(c("GroupA", "GroupB"), nrow(kernel_res$features), replace = TRUE)
wilcox_results <- wilcox_group_test(kernel_res$features, grouping)
head(wilcox_results)
top_features_plot(wilcox_results, top_n = 10)
```

```{r}
response_score <- setNames(rnorm(nrow(kernel_res$features)), rownames(kernel_res$features))
corr_results <- correlate_features_with_score(kernel_res$features, response_score)
head(corr_results)
correlation_plot(corr_results, top_n = 10)
```

### Monte Carlo method on the example data

```{r eval = FALSE}
set.seed(42)
mc_res <- compute_racing_montecarlo(
  input_data   = skcm_example,
  output_folder = tempdir(),
  file_name     = "skcm_example",
  nPatients     = 2,
  communication_type = "W",
  Ncells  = 100,
  Ngraphs = 5,
  Ndegree = 3,
  norm    = TRUE
)
```

content.content:
# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Project Overview

**RaCInG** (Random Cell-cell Interaction Generator) is an R package for reconstructing patient-specific cell-cell communication networks from bulk RNA-seq data. It implements two main workflows: a deterministic **kernel method** and a stochastic **Monte Carlo simulation** method.

Reference: van Santvoort et al. (2025, Cell Reports Methods)

## Development Commands

All standard R package development is done via `devtools` in an R session:

```r
devtools::load_all()        # Load package during development (replaces install)
devtools::check()           # Run R CMD check (equivalent to CI)
devtools::document()        # Regenerate NAMESPACE and man/*.Rd from roxygen2 comments
roxygen2::roxygenise()      # Alternative to devtools::document()
pkgdown::build_site()       # Build the documentation website locally
```

CI/CD runs `R CMD check --no-manual --compact-vignettes=gs+qpdf` on push/PR via GitHub Actions (`.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml`). Docs are auto-deployed via `.github/workflows/pkgdown.yaml`.

```r
devtools::test()            # Run the testthat regression suite (tests/testthat/)
```

The `testthat` suite (`tests/testthat/test-*.R`) covers correctness regressions across every module (network generation, kernel/Monte Carlo feature extraction, statistical analysis, txt/csv I/O, utilities) — run it after any change to `R/`, not just `R CMD check`.

## Architecture

### Two Core Workflows

**1. Kernel Method** (`R/Kernel_Method.R`)
- Entry point: `compute_racing_kernel(counts, ...)` or `compute_racing_kernel(input_data = ..., ...)`
- Computes a deterministic 3D kernel `[sender_cell × receiver_cell × patient]` via weighted matrix multiplication: `lig_weight %*% LRmatrix %*% t(rec_weight)`. The kernel is computed exactly once per call regardless of how many feature types are requested.
- Extracts network motif features from the kernel based on `communication_type` (`"D"`, `"W"`, `"TT"` — returns both trust- and cycle-triangle columns — or `"GSCC"`), which also accepts a character vector to extract several types from the same already-computed kernel in one call (`features` is then a named list, one data frame per type)
- Feature columns with no possible ligand-receptor pathway in any patient (structurally zero for every patient) are dropped automatically rather than returned as dead all-zero columns
- Returns `list(kernel, kernel_norm, features)`

**2. Monte Carlo Method** (`R/Monte_Carlo_Method.R`)
- Entry point: `compute_racing_montecarlo(input_data = ..., communication_type, Ncells, Ngraphs, Ndegree, ncores, ...)`
- For each patient, simulates `Ngraphs` random directed graph realizations (each with `Ncells` cells and target average degree `Ndegree`) via `model1()` (respects cell-type abundances & LR probabilities), then counts motifs on each realization
- `communication_type` accepts a vector (`"D"`, `"W"`, `"TT"`, `"CT"`, `"GSCC"`); when more than one is given, `countAllTypes()` extracts every requested type from the *same* simulated graphs instead of resimulating per type (`output` is then a named list, one entry per type)
- `ncores` parallelizes across patients (independent of each other) via `parallel`/`doParallel`/`foreach` — portable across Windows/macOS/Linux; workers are separate processes, so they use the *installed* package, not uncommitted `source()`-loaded changes
- Outputs mean/std of motif counts across realizations; optionally normalizes against a uniform random baseline
- Results written to `.out`/CSV files

### Data Flow

```
Raw Counts (genes × samples)
    ↓ prepare_input_files()   [R/RaCInG_input_generation.R]
    ├─ Lmatrix  (cells × ligands)
    ├─ Rmatrix  (cells × receptors)
    ├─ Cmatrix  (patients × cells, normalized abundances)
    └─ LRmatrix (ligands × receptors × patients)
    ↓
Kernel Method                  Monte Carlo Method
compute_kernel()               runSim() → model1() + motif counters
compute_kernel_features()      compute_results_processing()
    ↓
wilcox_group_test() → top_features_plot()
```

### Module Responsibilities

| File | Responsibility |
|------|---------------|
| `RaCInG_input_generation.R` | Preprocessing raw counts → standardized input matrices; CSV I/O |
| `Kernel_Method.R` | Deterministic kernel computation and feature extraction |
| `Monte_Carlo_Method.R` | Monte Carlo simulation orchestration |
| `network_generation.R` | Random directed graph generation (`model1()`) |
| `feature_extraction.R` | Graph motif enumeration (wedges, triangles, GSCC) |
| `Utilities.R` | Edge list ↔ adjacency matrix conversion; motif helpers |
| `statistical_analysis.R` | Wilcoxon group tests + ranked bar plots (`top_features_plot()`), Spearman correlation + rainfall plots (`correlation_plot()`) |
| `txt_to_csv.R` | Read/write simulation outputs |
| `data.R` | Documentation for bundled `skcm_example` dataset |

### Key Design Decisions

- **Sparse matrices**: `Matrix::sparseMatrix()` is used in Monte Carlo for memory-efficient adjacency matrices.
- **Optional heavy dependencies**: `prepare_input_files()` requires ADImpute, multideconv, OmnipathR, and liana — but all workflows accept pre-computed input matrices directly, making these optional.
- **Normalization**: Both the kernel and Monte Carlo methods can optionally compute a uniformized baseline (`norm`/`normalize`) to express features as an abundance-independent enrichment ratio, instead of raw communication strength.
- **Communication types**: `communication_type` controls which motif is extracted — `"D"` (direct), `"W"` (wedge/2-path), `"TT"` (trust triangle), `"CT"` (cycle triangle, Monte Carlo only as its own type — the kernel method returns it bundled with `"TT"`), `"GSCC"` (global strongly connected component). Both `compute_racing_kernel()` and `compute_racing_montecarlo()` accept a vector here to extract multiple types without redoing the expensive step (kernel computation / graph simulation) per type.
- **Vectorized, not looped, feature extraction**: `calculateWedges()`/`computeTriangles()` (kernel) and the array-reshape logic in `compute_results_processing()` (Monte Carlo) build the full combination grid up front and compute over it with matrix operations, instead of a triple-nested loop growing an R list one column at a time — the latter pattern is what makes cell-type counts in the hundreds (where wedge/triangle combinations reach 10^5-10^6) crash or hang.
- **Column naming is shared across methods**: kernel and Monte Carlo feature matrices use identical column-naming conventions (`"Dir_A_B"`, `"W_A_B_C"`, etc.) and real patient IDs as rownames, so their outputs can be fed into the same downstream statistical/plotting functions interchangeably.

### Example Data

`skcm_example` (in `data/skcm_example.rda`) is pre-processed TCGA skin cutaneous melanoma data: 10 patients × 9 cell types × 276 ligands × 298 receptors. Use it for testing and examples.

### Verified Against the Original Python Implementation

The companion project at `~/Documents/Racing_paper` (`scripts/Melanoma_RaCInG_R_portcheck.qmd`,
`scripts/RaCInG_original_melanoma.ipynb`, `scripts/Compare_RaCInG_R_vs_original.qmd`) verified
that `compute_kernel()`/`calculateDirect()`/`calculateWedges()`/`computeTriangles()` reproduce
the original, unmodified Python implementation's math exactly on the full 336-patient melanoma
cohort — Pearson r = 1 and relative differences at machine precision for all three feature
families. Two real (non-bug) differences to be aware of when comparing outputs against the
original Python code:
- The original's `calculateDirect()`/`calculateWedges()`/`calculateTriangles()` internally
  truncate `"CD8+ T"` → `"CD8"` before building column labels; this R port does not.
- `calculateWedges()` here labels columns `"W_{free}_{hub}_{k}"`; the original Python labels
  the same triple (identical values) `"W_{hub}_{free}_{k}"` — a naming-convention difference
  only, not a math difference.

### Known Design Gap: Feature Column Identity

`calculateDirect()`/`calculateWedges()`/`computeTriangles()` return sender/receiver cell-type
identity only baked into a glued column-name string (`"Dir_A_B"`, `"W_A_B_C"`) — never as
structured columns (e.g. `CellA`/`CellB`) alongside the values. Every downstream caller that
needs the identity separately (e.g. "does this pair involve cell type X, in either position")
has to reconstruct it by rebuilding the same name in the same internal iteration order and
matching against `colnames()` — this exact reconstruction has been independently reimplemented
at least three times in the companion `Racing_paper` project. Consider having these functions
return the pair identity as real columns (or an attached attribute) directly, so callers don't

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Project Overview

**RaCInG** (Random Cell-cell Interaction Generator) is an R package for reconstructing patient-specific cell-cell communication networks from bulk RNA-seq data. It implements two main workflows: a deterministic **kernel method** and a stochastic **Monte Carlo simulation** method.

Reference: van Santvoort et al. (2025, Cell Reports Methods)

## Development Commands

All standard R package development is done via `devtools` in an R session:

```r
devtools::load_all()        # Load package during development (replaces install)
devtools::check()           # Run R CMD check (equivalent to CI)
devtools::document()        # Regenerate NAMESPACE and man/*.Rd from roxygen2 comments
roxygen2::roxygenise()      # Alternative to devtools::document()
pkgdown::build_site()       # Build the documentation website locally
```

CI/CD runs `R CMD check --no-manual --compact-vignettes=gs+qpdf` on push/PR via GitHub Actions (`.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml`). Docs are auto-deployed via `.github/workflows/pkgdown.yaml`.

```r
devtools::test()            # Run the testthat regression suite (tests/testthat/)
```

The `testthat` suite (`tests/testthat/test-*.R`) covers correctness regressions across every module (network generation, kernel/Monte Carlo feature extraction, statistical analysis, txt/csv I/O, utilities) — run it after any change to `R/`, not just `R CMD check`.

## Architecture

### Two Core Workflows

**1. Kernel Method** (`R/Kernel_Method.R`)
- Entry point: `compute_racing_kernel(counts, ...)` or `compute_racing_kernel(input_data = ..., ...)`
- Computes a deterministic 3D kernel `[sender_cell × receiver_cell × patient]` via weighted matrix multiplication: `lig_weight %*% LRmatrix %*% t(rec_weight)`. The kernel is computed exactly once per call regardless of how many feature types are requested.
- Extracts network motif features from the kernel based on `communication_type` (`"D"`, `"W"`, `"TT"` — returns both trust- and cycle-triangle columns — or `"GSCC"`), which also accepts a character vector to extract several types from the same already-computed kernel in one call (`features` is then a named list, one data frame per type)
- Feature columns with no possible ligand-receptor pathway in any patient (structurally zero for every patient) are dropped automatically rather than returned as dead all-zero columns
- Returns `list(kernel, kernel_norm, features)`

**2. Monte Carlo Method** (`R/Monte_Carlo_Method.R`)
- Entry point: `compute_racing_montecarlo(input_data = ..., communication_type, Ncells, Ngraphs, Ndegree, ncores, ...)`
- For each patient, simulates `Ngraphs` random directed graph realizations (each with `Ncells` cells and target average degree `Ndegree`) via `model1()` (respects cell-type abundances & LR probabilities), then counts motifs on each realization
- `communication_type` accepts a vector (`"D"`, `"W"`, `"TT"`, `"CT"`, `"GSCC"`); when more than one is given, `countAllTypes()` extracts every requested type from the *same* simulated graphs instead of resimulating per type (`output` is then a named list, one entry per type)
- `ncores` parallelizes across patients (independent of each other) via `parallel`/`doParallel`/`foreach` — portable across Windows/macOS/Linux; workers are separate processes, so they use the *installed* package, not uncommitted `source()`-loaded changes
- Outputs mean/std of motif counts across realizations; optionally normalizes against a uniform random baseline
- Results written to `.out`/CSV files

### Data Flow

```
Raw Counts (genes × samples)
    ↓ prepare_input_files()   [R/RaCInG_input_generation.R]
    ├─ Lmatrix  (cells × ligands)
    ├─ Rmatrix  (cells × receptors)
    ├─ Cmatrix  (patients × cells, normalized abundances)
    └─ LRmatrix (ligands × receptors × patients)
    ↓
Kernel Method                  Monte Carlo Method
compute_kernel()               runSim() → model1() + motif counters
compute_kernel_features()      compute_results_processing()
    ↓
wilcox_group_test() → top_features_plot()
```

### Module Responsibilities

| File | Responsibility |
|------|---------------|
| `RaCInG_input_generation.R` | Preprocessing raw counts → standardized input matrices; CSV I/O |
| `Kernel_Method.R` | Deterministic kernel computation and feature extraction |
| `Monte_Carlo_Method.R` | Monte Carlo simulation orchestration |
| `network_generation.R` | Random directed graph generation (`model1()`) |
| `feature_extraction.R` | Graph motif enumeration (wedges, triangles, GSCC) |
| `Utilities.R` | Edge list ↔ adjacency matrix conversion; motif helpers |
| `statistical_analysis.R` | Wilcoxon group tests + ranked bar plots (`top_features_plot()`), Spearman correlation + rainfall plots (`correlation_plot()`) |
| `txt_to_csv.R` | Read/write simulation outputs |
| `data.R` | Documentation for bundled `skcm_example` dataset |

### Key Design Decisions

- **Sparse matrices**: `Matrix::sparseMatrix()` is used in Monte Carlo for memory-efficient adjacency matrices.
- **Optional heavy dependencies**: `prepare_input_files()` requires ADImpute, multideconv, OmnipathR, and liana — but all workflows accept pre-computed input matrices directly, making these optional.
- **Normalization**: Both the kernel and Monte Carlo methods can optionally compute a uniformized baseline (`norm`/`normalize`) to express features as an abundance-independent enrichment ratio, instead of raw communication strength.
- **Communication types**: `communication_type` controls which motif is extracted — `"D"` (direct), `"W"` (wedge/2-path), `"TT"` (trust triangle), `"CT"` (cycle triangle, Monte Carlo only as its own type — the kernel method returns it bundled with `"TT"`), `"GSCC"` (global strongly connected component). Both `compute_racing_kernel()` and `compute_racing_montecarlo()` accept a vector here to extract multiple types without redoing the expensive step (kernel computation / graph simulation) per type.
- **Vectorized, not looped, feature extraction**: `calculateWedges()`/`computeTriangles()` (kernel) and the array-reshape logic in `compute_results_processing()` (Monte Carlo) build the full combination grid up front and compute over it with matrix operations, instead of a triple-nested loop growing an R list one column at a time — the latter pattern is what makes cell-type counts in the hundreds (where wedge/triangle combinations reach 10^5-10^6) crash or hang.
- **Column naming is shared across methods**: kernel and Monte Carlo feature matrices use identical column-naming conventions (`"Dir_A_B"`, `"W_A_B_C"`, etc.) and real patient IDs as rownames, so their outputs can be fed into the same downstream statistical/plotting functions interchangeably.

### Example Data

`skcm_example` (in `data/skcm_example.rda`) is pre-processed TCGA skin cutaneous melanoma data: 10 patients × 9 cell types × 276 ligands × 298 receptors. Use it for testing and examples.

### Verified Against the Original Python Implementation

The companion project at `~/Documents/Racing_paper` (`scripts/Melanoma_RaCInG_R_portcheck.qmd`,
`scripts/RaCInG_original_melanoma.ipynb`, `scripts/Compare_RaCInG_R_vs_original.qmd`) verified
that `compute_kernel()`/`calculateDirect()`/`calculateWedges()`/`computeTriangles()` reproduce
the original, unmodified Python implementation's math exactly on the full 336-patient melanoma
cohort — Pearson r = 1 and relative differences at machine precision for all three feature
families. Two real (non-bug) differences to be aware of when comparing outputs against the
original Python code:
- The original's `calculateDirect()`/`calculateWedges()`/`calculateTriangles()` internally
  truncate `"CD8+ T"` → `"CD8"` before building column labels; this R port does not.
- `calculateWedges()` here labels columns `"W_{free}_{hub}_{k}"`; the original Python labels
  the same triple (identical values) `"W_{hub}_{free}_{k}"` — a naming-convention difference
  only, not a math difference.

### Known Design Gap: Feature Column Identity

`calculateDirect()`/`calculateWedges()`/`computeTriangles()` return sender/receiver cell-type
identity only baked into a glued column-name string (`"Dir_A_B"`, `"W_A_B_C"`) — never as
structured columns (e.g. `CellA`/`CellB`) alongside the values. Every downstream caller that
needs the identity separately (e.g. "does this pair involve cell type X, in either position")
has to reconstruct it by rebuilding the same name in the same internal iteration order and
matching against `colnames()` — this exact reconstruction has been independently reimplemented
at least three times in the companion `Racing_paper` project. Consider having these functions
return the pair identity as real columns (or an attached attribute) directly, so callers don't
need to reverse-engineer a string this package itself constructed.

89	#' Read and normalize cell-type abundance estimates
90	#'
91	#' @param cells Character vector of expected cell types.
92	#' @param filename Path to a CSV file containing patient-by-cell-type abundances.
93	#'
94	#' @return A list with the normalized `Dtypes` matrix plus labels.
95	#' @export
96	createCellTypeDistr <- function(cells, filename) {
97	  if (!file.exists(filename)) {
98	    stop("Cell type distribution file does not exist...")
99	  }
100	  
101	  # Read CSV file, using the first column as rownames (datasets)
102	  df <- utils::read.csv(filename, row.names = 1)
103	  
104	  # Extract column names as cell type names and row names as dataset/patient names
105	  celltypes <- colnames(df)
106	  datasets <- rownames(df)
107	
108	  # Convert the data frame to a numeric matrix, keeping dataset names as rownames
109	  # so downstream functions (e.g. compute_racing_montecarlo) can recover patient IDs
110	  Dtypes <- as.matrix(df)
111	  storage.mode(Dtypes) <- "numeric"
112	  rownames(Dtypes) <- datasets
113	
114	  # Normalize rows so each dataset sums to 1 (relative fractions)
115	  row_sums <- rowSums(Dtypes)
116	  normalized <- Dtypes / row_sums
117	
118	  # Sort cell types alphabetically
119	  sp <- sortPermute(celltypes)
120	  celltypes <- sp$sortlist
121	  perm <- sp$perm
122	  Dtypes <- normalized[, perm, drop = FALSE]
123	
124	  # Restrict to the cell types that actually appear in Lmatrix/Rmatrix.
125	  # ccc_table's expression threshold can leave some cell types with no
126	  # ligand/receptor pair at all (they never send or receive anything above
127	  # threshold), so `cells` (from Lmatrix) can be a strict subset of the
128	  # deconvolution's full cell-type vocabulary. Those cell types contribute
129	  # nothing to the network, so they're dropped from Cmatrix here rather than
130	  # left in as columns with no matching Lmatrix/Rmatrix row.
131	  if (length(cells) != length(celltypes)) {
132	    if (!all(cells %in% celltypes)) {
133	      stop("Cell types in Lmatrix/Rmatrix are not a subset of Cmatrix's cell types -- mismatched input files.")
134	    }
135	    keep <- celltypes %in% cells
136	    Dtypes <- Dtypes[, keep, drop = FALSE]
137	    celltypes <- celltypes[keep]
138	    Dtypes <- Dtypes / rowSums(Dtypes) # re-normalize so each dataset still sums to 1 after dropping cell types with no active ligand/receptor
139	  }
140	
141	  return(list(Dtypes = Dtypes,
142	              celltypes = celltypes,
143	              datasets = datasets))
144	}

146	#' Read ligand-receptor interaction probabilities
147	#'
148	#' @param filename Path to a CSV file containing patient-by-interaction weights.
149	#' @param ligands Character vector of ligand names.
150	#' @param receptors Character vector of receptor names.
151	#'
152	#' @return A 3D array with dimensions ligand × receptor × patient.
153	#' @export
154	createInteractionDistr <- function(filename, ligands, receptors) {
155	  if (!file.exists(filename)) {
156	    stop("Interaction distribution file does not exist...")
157	  }
158	  
159	  df <- utils::read.csv(filename, row.names = 1)
160	  
161	  # Store column names (interaction names like LIG_REC) and row names (datasets)
162	  interactions <- colnames(df)
163	  datasets <- rownames(df)
164	  
165	  # Convert data frame to numeric matrix, replacing NA values with 0
166	  distr <- df %>%
167	    tibble::rownames_to_column("Datasets") %>%
168	    dplyr::select(-Datasets) %>%
169	    dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(
170	      dplyr::everything(),                      # apply to all columns
171	      ~ tidyr::replace_na(as.numeric(.), 0)     # convert to numeric and replace NA with 0
172	    )) %>%
173	    as.matrix() 
174	  
175	  # Split interaction names "LIG_REC" into ligand and receptor parts
176	  parts <- strsplit(interactions, "_")
177	  rowWordIndex <- sapply(parts, `[`, 1)
178	  colWordIndex <- sapply(parts, `[`, 2)
179	  
180	  # Convert ligand/receptor names into numeric indices matching the provided ligand/receptor lists
181	  row <- match(rowWordIndex, ligands)
182	  col <- match(colWordIndex, receptors)
183	  
184	  # Create a 3D tensor to hold ligand-receptor probabilities
185	  # Dimensions: ligands x receptors x datasets
186	  DconnectionTensor <- array(0, dim = c(length(ligands), length(receptors), nrow(distr)))
187	  
188	  # Fill the tensor: for each dataset, assign probability values to the correct ligand-receptor pairs
189	  for (i in 1:nrow(distr)) {
190	    DconnectionTensor[cbind(row, col, i)] <- distr[i, ]
191	  }
192	  
193	  # Normalize each dataset slice so that the sum of all probabilities equals 1
194	  # This ensures that each dataset represents a valid probability distribution over all ligand-receptor pairs
195	  normsum <- apply(DconnectionTensor, 3, sum)
196	  
197	  for (i in 1:length(normsum)) {
198	    if (normsum[i] != 0) { # avoids division by 0
199	      DconnectionTensor[, , i] <- DconnectionTensor[, , i] / normsum[i]
200	    }
201	  }
202	  
203	  # Return the normalized 3D tensor
204	  return(DconnectionTensor)
205	}

345	  canonical <- c(

347	    "Macrophages.M0", "Macrophages.M1", "Macrophages.M2", "Macrophages.cells",
348	    "Monocytes", "Neutrophils",

351	    "CD4.non.regulatory", "CD4.regulatory", "CD4.cells", "CD8.cells",
352	    "T.cells.helper", "T.cells.gamma.delta",
353	    "Dendritic.activated.cells", "Dendritic.resting.cells", "Dendritic.cells",
354	    "Cancer", "Endothelial", "Eosinophils", "Plasma", "Myocytes",
355	    "Fibroblasts", "Mast.activated.cells", "Mast.resting.cells", "Mast.cells",
356	    "CAF", "uncharacterized_cell"
357	  )
358	  canonical <- canonical[order(-nchar(canonical))]  # longest match wins
359	
360	  vapply(x, function(nm) {
361	    hit <- canonical[endsWith(nm, canonical)]
362	    if (length(hit) > 0) hit[1] else nm
363	  }, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
364	}

366	#' Estimate per-cell-type average expression profiles from one composition
367	#'
368	#' For each gene, solves a non-negative least squares regression of bulk TPM
369	#' expression across samples against per-sample cell-type fractions, giving
370	#' one expression value per gene per cell type:
371	#' `bulk_expr[gene, sample] ~= sum_celltype fractions[sample, celltype] * profile[gene, celltype]`.
372	#' Valid only when every column of `deconv` already belongs to one coherent
373	#' composition (fractions summing to ~1 per sample). When `deconv` instead
374	#' spans multiple deconvolution methods/signatures concatenated together (as
375	#' `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()` produces before subgroup analysis),
376	#' use [.estimate_expression_profiles_subgroups()] instead -- fitting NNLS
377	#' directly across method/signature blocks here would violate the mixture
378	#' equation this regression assumes.
379	#'
380	#' @param counts_tpm Gene-by-sample TPM matrix.
381	#' @param deconv Sample-by-cell-type fraction matrix.
382	#'
383	#' @return A gene-by-cell-type data frame of estimated expression profiles.
384	#' @keywords internal
385	.estimate_expression_profiles_samples <- function(counts_tpm, deconv) {
386	  samples <- intersect(colnames(counts_tpm), rownames(deconv))
387	  X <- as.matrix(deconv[samples, , drop = FALSE])
388	  Y <- as.matrix(counts_tpm[, samples, drop = FALSE])
389	
390	  profile <- matrix(0, nrow = nrow(Y), ncol = ncol(X),
391	                    dimnames = list(rownames(Y), colnames(X)))
392	  for (g in seq_len(nrow(Y))) {
393	    profile[g, ] <- stats::coef(nnls::nnls(X, Y[g, ]))
394	  }
395	
396	  as.data.frame(profile)
397	}
398	
399	#' Estimate per-cell-type expression profiles across multiple deconvolution
400	#' methods/signatures
401	#'
402	#' `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()`'s raw output concatenates one block
403	#' of columns per method-signature combination (named
404	#' `"{method}_{signature}_{celltype}"`). Each block is, on its own, a valid
405	#' composition -- multideconv itself verifies every block's standardized
406	#' cell-type columns sum to 1 per sample -- but
407	#' `multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis()`'s merged "Deconvolution
408	#' matrix" is not: it stitches together representatives from different blocks
409	#' per cell type, so fitting [.estimate_expression_profiles_samples()]'s NNLS
410	#' mixture equation directly on it is invalid. This instead fits one profile
411	#' per method-signature block (always a valid composition), then merges the
412	#' resulting *profiles* -- never the raw fractions -- according to whichever
413	#' subgroups `subgroups` (already computed by the caller via
414	#' `multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis()`) forms across those blocks.
415	#'
416	#' A subgroup formed in a later merge iteration can list an earlier
417	#' iteration's subgroup name as one of its own members, not just raw columns
418	#' -- this is unwound the same way multideconv's own (retired)
419	#' `expand_subgroup_members()` helper does, by repeatedly replacing any nested
420	#' subgroup reference with its members until only raw columns remain, then
421	#' merging via one flat median across all of them.
422	#'
423	#' @param counts_tpm Gene-by-sample TPM matrix.
424	#' @param deconv_wide Sample-by-`{method}_{signature}_{celltype}` raw fraction
425	#'   matrix -- `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()`'s direct output, before
426	#'   subgroup analysis.
427	#' @param subgroups The list returned by
428	#'   `multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis(deconv_wide)`.
429	#'
430	#' @return A gene-by-cell-type data frame of estimated expression profiles,
431	#'   one column per feature surviving in `subgroups[["Deconvolution matrix"]]`.
432	#' @keywords internal
433	.estimate_expression_profiles_subgroups <- function(counts_tpm, deconv_wide, subgroups) {
434	  block_id <- sub("^([^_]+_[^_]+)_.+$", "\\1", colnames(deconv_wide))
435	
436	  profiles_by_block <- lapply(split(colnames(deconv_wide), block_id), function(cols) {
437	    as.matrix(.estimate_expression_profiles_samples(counts_tpm, deconv_wide[, cols, drop = FALSE]))
438	  })
439	
440	  common_genes <- Reduce(intersect, lapply(profiles_by_block, rownames))
441	  all_profiles <- do.call(cbind, lapply(profiles_by_block, function(p) p[common_genes, , drop = FALSE]))
442	
443	  # compute_subgroups() (called inside compute.deconvolution.analysis(), which
444	  # produced `subgroups`) converts its input through data.frame() internally,
445	  # which sanitizes column names via make.names() -- e.g. a hyphenated
446	  # signature name like "CBSX-HNSCC-scRNAseq" becomes "CBSX.HNSCC.scRNAseq".
447	  # So the Deconvolution matrix's columns and every subgroup's member names
448	  # already come back sanitized; all_profiles (built directly from
449	  # deconv_wide's raw, un-sanitized names) needs the same treatment to match.
450	  colnames(all_profiles) <- make.names(colnames(all_profiles))
451	
452	  dt <- subgroups[["Deconvolution matrix"]]
453	  groups <- subgroups[["Deconvolution subgroups composition"]]
454	
455	  subgroup_lookup <- list()
456	  for (bucket in names(groups)) {
457	    bucket_groups <- groups[[bucket]]
458	    for (subgroup_name in names(bucket_groups)) {
459	      subgroup_lookup[[subgroup_name]] <- bucket_groups[[subgroup_name]]
460	    }
461	  }
462	
463	  expand_subgroup_members <- function(members, subgroup_map) {
464	    while (any(members %in% names(subgroup_map))) {
465	      members <- unlist(lapply(members, function(m) {
466	        if (m %in% names(subgroup_map)) subgroup_map[[m]] else m
467	      }), use.names = FALSE)
468	    }
469	    members
470	  }
471	
472	  merged <- sapply(colnames(dt), function(feature) {
473	    raw_cols <- if (feature %in% names(subgroup_lookup)) {
474	      expand_subgroup_members(subgroup_lookup[[feature]], subgroup_lookup)
475	    } else if (feature %in% colnames(all_profiles)) {
476	      feature
477	    } else {
478	      stop("Deconvolution feature '", feature, "' could not be traced back to any ",
479	           "original method-signature column or subgroup -- naming mismatch between ",
480	           "compute.deconvolution.analysis() output and deconv_wide.")
481	    }
482	    apply(as.matrix(all_profiles[, raw_cols, drop = FALSE]), 1, stats::median)
483	  })
484	  dimnames(merged) <- list(common_genes, colnames(dt))
485	
486	  stopifnot(ncol(merged) == ncol(dt))
487	  as.data.frame(merged)
488	}
489	
490	#' Build RaCInG input files from raw count data
491	#'
492	#' This function combines the preprocessing and input-loading steps into a single
493	#' call. It generates the `L`, `R`, `C`, and `LR` CSV files from raw counts,
494	#' then reads them back to produce the normalised matrices and 3-D tensor required
495	#' by the kernel and Monte Carlo workflows.
496	#'
497	#' @param counts Gene-by-sample count matrix.
498	#' @param output_folder Directory where the generated `L`, `R`, `C`, and `LR` files are written.
499	#' @param deconv Optional patient-by-cell-type abundance matrix. If omitted, it
500	#'   is computed via `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()` followed by
501	#'   `multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis()` (which identifies and
502	#'   collapses correlated cell-type subgroups) and
503	#'   `multideconv::standardize_celltype_colnames()`.
504	#' @param cc_network Optional ligand-receptor prior network. If omitted, it is
505	#'   retrieved via `liana::get_curated_omni()` (a curated, OmniPath-backed
506	#'   consensus of CellPhoneDB/CellChatDB/ICELLNET/connectomeDB2020/CellTalkDB)
507	#'   the first time this is called, then cached indefinitely as an RDS file
508	#'   under `tools::R_user_dir("RaCInG", "cache")` and loaded from there on every
509	#'   subsequent call -- avoiding a live network round-trip (and its associated
510	#'   transient-failure risk) on every invocation. Delete that cache file to
511	#'   force a refresh from OmniPath.
512	#' @param fun_LR Function combining a ligand's and receptor's expression
513	#'   values (as a length-2 vector) into one interaction strength. Default
514	#'   `min`: the weaker-expressed partner limits the interaction. Any function
515	#'   collapsing 2 values to 1 works, e.g. `prod` for the product of the two
516	#'   instead.
517	#' @param cell_expr_profile Optional gene-by-cell-type expression profile
518	#'   matrix. If omitted, it is estimated via per-gene non-negative least
519	#'   squares -- per method-signature block, then merged according to the
520	#'   multideconv subgroup analysis, when `deconv` is auto-computed (see
521	#'   `.estimate_expression_profiles_subgroups()`), or directly from the
522	#'   supplied `deconv` otherwise (see `.estimate_expression_profiles_samples()`).
523	#' @param source,target Column names to use as ligand and receptor identifiers when `cc_network` is supplied.
524	#' @param deconv_method Deconvolution method(s) passed to `multideconv::compute.deconvolution()`.
525	#' @param cbsx.name,cbsx.token Optional credentials forwarded to the deconvolution workflow.
526	#' @param file_name File stem used when exporting the generated CSV files.
527	#' @param signed Logical; if `TRUE`, also try to load a sign matrix from `output_folder`.
528	#'
529	#' @param already_normalized Logical; if `TRUE`, `counts` is treated as
530	#'   already TPM-normalized, **linear scale, not logged**, and the internal
531	#'   `ADImpute::NormalizeTPM()` gene-length/library-size normalization is
532	#'   skipped. Use this for datasets where only pre-normalized expression is
533	#'   available (e.g. public cohorts distributed as log2(TPM+1) matrices with
534	#'   no raw counts -- convert those back to linear scale, e.g. `2^x - 1`,
535	#'   before passing them here) -- applying `NormalizeTPM()` to already-
536	#'   normalized data would re-apply its gene-length correction on top of the
537	#'   original normalization, distorting relative gene expression levels.
538	#'   Emits a warning, since `expr_threshold` below is only meaningful if this
539	#'   linear-scale assumption holds -- comparing a log-scale value against it
540	#'   would silently apply the wrong cutoff.
541	#'
542	#' @param expr_threshold Minimum expression value, in linear-scale TPM (in
543	#'   `cell_expr_profile` units), a ligand or receptor must reach in its
544	#'   sending/receiving cell type for that ligand-receptor-celltype triple to
545	#'   be kept in `CC_table`.
546	#'
547	#' @return A named list with the processed input matrices and their labels:
548	#'   `Lmatrix`, `Rmatrix`, `Cmatrix` (normalised), `LRmatrix` (3-D tensor),
549	#'   `celltypes`, `ligands`, `receptors`, `Sign_matrix`, and `CC_table`.
550	#' @export
551	prepare_input_files <- function(counts, output_folder = "Results/", deconv = NULL, cc_network = NULL, fun_LR = min,
552	                                cell_expr_profile = NULL, source = "source_genesymbol", target = "target_genesymbol",
553	                                deconv_method = "Quantiseq", cbsx.name = NULL, cbsx.token = NULL, file_name = NULL,
554	                                signed = FALSE, already_normalized = FALSE, expr_threshold = 10){
555	
556	  if (is.null(file_name)) {
557	    file_name <- "RaCInG_input"
558	  }
559	
560	  .check_installed_packages(c("ADImpute", "multideconv"))
561	  if (already_normalized) {
562	    warning(
563	      "already_normalized = TRUE: 'counts' is assumed to already be linear-scale TPM. ",
564	      "expr_threshold (default ", expr_threshold, ") is compared against this scale -- ",
565	      "if 'counts' is actually log-transformed (e.g. log2(TPM+1)), that comparison is ",
566	      "wrong; convert back to linear TPM first or set expr_threshold accordingly.",
567	      call. = FALSE
568	    )
569	    counts.tpm <- as.matrix(counts)
570	  } else {
571	    counts.tpm <- ADImpute::NormalizeTPM(counts)
572	  }
573	  counts.log.tpm <- log2(counts.tpm + 1)
574	
575	  cat("Calculating deconvolution estimates...\n")
576	
577	  ## C-matrix
578	  # deconv_wide/subgroups stay NULL on the user-supplied-deconv path below --
579	  # there's no known method/signature block structure to fit expression
580	  # profiles per block, so that path falls back to treating the whole matrix
581	  # as one composition (see the expression-profile step further down).
582	  deconv_wide <- NULL
583	  subgroups <- NULL
584	  if (is.null(deconv)) {
585	    deconv_wide <- multideconv::compute.deconvolution(
586	      counts.tpm,
587	      normalized = FALSE,
588	      methods = deconv_method,
589	      credentials.mail = cbsx.name,
590	      credentials.token = cbsx.token,
591	      file_name = file_name
592	    )
593	
594	    ## Verify patient names match between files before running the subgroup analysis
595	    if (!all(rownames(deconv_wide) %in% colnames(counts))) {
596	      stop("Patient names in deconvolution estimates do not match those in the counts matrix.")
597	    }
598	
599	    cat("Identifying cell type subgroups...\n")
600	    subgroups <- multideconv::compute.deconvolution.analysis(deconv_wide)
601	    deconv <- subgroups[["Deconvolution matrix"]]
602	  } else {
603	    cat("Using provided deconvolution estimates...\n")
604	    if (!all(rownames(deconv) %in% colnames(counts))) {
605	      stop("Patient names in deconvolution estimates do not match those in the counts matrix.")
606	    }
607	  }
608	
609	  ## Cell type expression profiles
610	  cat("\nEstimating cell type expression profiles...\n")
611	  if (is.null(cell_expr_profile)) {
612	    .check_installed_packages("nnls")
613	    if (!is.null(deconv_wide)) {
614	      # Fit one profile per method-signature block (each a valid composition),
615	      # then merge according to whichever subgroups multideconv formed --
616	      # never fit NNLS directly on the merged Deconvolution matrix (`deconv`),
617	      # which stitches together representatives from different blocks and is
618	      # not itself a valid composition. See .estimate_expression_profiles_subgroups().
619	      cell_expr_profile <- .estimate_expression_profiles_subgroups(counts.tpm, deconv_wide, subgroups)
620	    } else {
621	      # A user-supplied deconv has no known block structure -- treat it as one
622	      # composition, as before.
623	      cell_expr_profile <- .estimate_expression_profiles_samples(counts.tpm, deconv)
624	    }
625	  }
626	
627	  ## Prior knowledge network CC
628	  cat("Processing cell-cell interaction network...\n")
629	  if (is.null(cc_network)) {
630	    .check_installed_packages(c("OmnipathR", "liana"))
631	    cache_dir <- tools::R_user_dir("RaCInG", "cache")
632	    cache_file <- file.path(cache_dir, "curated_omni_network.rds")
633	    if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
634	      cc_network <- readRDS(cache_file)
635	    } else {
636	      # get_curated_omni()'s underlying calls hit OmnipathR's own on-disk cache for
637	      # most of the network data, but at least one internal step (parameter
638	      # validation against OmnipathR::resources()) always makes a live request
639	      # regardless -- so this whole result is still subject to transient network
640	      # failures on every fresh R session unless cached at this level too.
641	      cc_network <- liana::get_curated_omni() %>%
642	        dplyr::filter(category_intercell_source %in% c("cell_surface_ligand", "ligand") & #check why not adhesion also or ecm
643	                      category_intercell_target %in% c("receptor", "adhesion")) %>%
644	        liana::decomplexify(columns = c("source_genesymbol", "target_genesymbol"))
645	      dir.create(cache_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
646	      saveRDS(cc_network, cache_file)
647	    }
648	  } else {
649	    cc_network <- cc_network %>%
650	      dplyr::mutate(source_genesymbol = .data[[source]], target_genesymbol = .data[[target]])
651	  }
652	  
653	  ## Subset expression for LR pairs (keep only interactions present in cell_expr_profile)
654	  keep <- integer()
655	  for (i in seq_len(nrow(cc_network))) {
656	    ligand  <- cc_network$source_genesymbol[i]
657	    receptor <- cc_network$target_genesymbol[i]
658	    if (ligand %in% rownames(cell_expr_profile) & receptor %in% rownames(cell_expr_profile)) {
659	      keep <- c(keep, i)
660	    }
661	  }
662	  cc_interations_sub <- cc_network[keep, , drop = FALSE]
663	  
664	  ## Build CC table (Sender x each LR pair x Receiver)
665	  ## Vectorized and processed one sender at a time: the previous implementation
666	  ## built one data.frame per (cell_type, LR pair) via nested
667	  ## do.call(rbind, lapply(...)) calls, i.e. O(n_celltypes * n_LR_pairs) tiny
668	  ## data.frames rbound together. With many deconvolution features (e.g.
669	  ## combining several deconvolution methods) n_celltypes can reach 100+, and
670	  ## with a curated LR network of several thousand pairs this produced
671	  ## hundreds of thousands of rbind pieces and tens of millions of rows, slow
672	  ## enough (tens of minutes) and memory-heavy enough to crash on typical
673	  ## machines. A single vectorized pass across the full sender x LR x receiver
674	  ## grid fixed the speed but still peaks at O(n_celltypes^2 * n_LR_pairs)
675	  ## elements transiently (~15GB observed with 122 cell types, i.e. the
676	  ## machine's entire RAM) before the expression-threshold filter shrinks it
677	  ## back down. Building one sender's full receiver grid at a time and
678	  ## filtering immediately keeps peak memory at O(n_celltypes * n_LR_pairs)
679	  ## instead, independent of how many senders there are.
680	  celltypes_all <- colnames(cell_expr_profile)
681	  n_ct <- length(celltypes_all)
682	  n_lr <- nrow(cc_interations_sub)
683	  cell_expr_mat <- as.matrix(cell_expr_profile)
684	  L_all <- cc_interations_sub$source_genesymbol
685	  R_all <- cc_interations_sub$target_genesymbol
686	  L_row <- match(L_all, rownames(cell_expr_mat))
687	  R_row <- match(R_all, rownames(cell_expr_mat))
688	
689	  lr_idx_rep       <- rep(seq_len(n_lr), each = n_ct)
690	  receiver_idx_rep <- rep(seq_len(n_ct), times = n_lr)
691	  R_row_rep        <- R_row[lr_idx_rep]
692	
693	  ccc_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n_ct), function(s) {
694	    Expr_Ligand   <- cell_expr_mat[L_row[lr_idx_rep], s]
695	    Expr_Receptor <- cell_expr_mat[cbind(R_row_rep, receiver_idx_rep)]
696	    keep <- Expr_Ligand >= expr_threshold & Expr_Receptor >= expr_threshold ## Keep only pairs expressed above threshold
697	    data.frame(
698	      Sender = rep(celltypes_all[s], sum(keep)),
699	      Ligand = L_all[lr_idx_rep[keep]],
700	      Expr_Ligand = Expr_Ligand[keep],
701	      Receiver = celltypes_all[receiver_idx_rep[keep]],
702	      Receptor = R_all[lr_idx_rep[keep]],
703	      Expr_Receptor = Expr_Receptor[keep]
704	    )
705	  }))
706	
707	  ## Use the actual matched (Ligand, Receptor) pairs present in ccc_table --
708	  ## previously this zipped unique(Ligand) with unique(Receptor) positionally,
709	  ## silently mismatching real pairs whenever the two vectors had different
710	  ## lengths (recycling warning: "number of columns of result is not a
711	  ## multiple of vector length").
712	  lr_pairs_df <- unique(ccc_table[, c("Ligand", "Receptor")])
713	  ligands <- lr_pairs_df$Ligand
714	  receptors <- lr_pairs_df$Receptor
715	  LR_pairs <- paste0(ligands, "_", receptors)
716	
717	  ## LR-matrix: compute fun(L, R) per sample using counts (rows=genes, cols=samples): Default min(L,R)
718	  cat("Computing LR matrix...\n")
719	  pos_lr <- match(c(rbind(ligands, receptors)), rownames(counts.log.tpm))
720	  pos_lr <- matrix(pos_lr, nrow = 2)
721	  
722	  LR_matrix <- apply(pos_lr, 2, function(idx) {
723	    if (any(is.na(idx))) {
724	      return(rep(NA, ncol(counts.log.tpm)))
725	    }
726	    apply(counts.log.tpm[idx, , drop = FALSE], 2, function(x) fun_LR(x))
727	  })
728	  colnames(LR_matrix) <- LR_pairs
729	  rownames(LR_matrix) <- gsub(".", "-", rownames(LR_matrix), fixed = TRUE)
730	  
731	  ## L-matrix: ligands vs cell types compatibility (from filtered cc table) ## how do you know which ligand is expressed in which cell type? there is no database?
732	  cat("Computing L-matrix...\n")
733	  celltypes <- unique(ccc_table$Sender)
734	  ligs <- unique(ccc_table$Ligand)
735	  Lmatrix <- matrix(0, nrow = length(celltypes), ncol = length(ligs),
736	                    dimnames = list(celltypes, ligs))
737	  for (ct in celltypes) {
738	    tmp <- ccc_table %>% dplyr::filter(Sender == ct) %>% dplyr::select(Ligand) %>% unique()
739	    Lmatrix[ct, tmp$Ligand] <- 1
740	  }
741	  
742	  ## R-matrix: receptors vs cell types compatibility
743	  cat("Computing R-matrix...\n")
744	  recs <- unique(ccc_table$Receptor)
745	  Rmatrix <- matrix(0, nrow = length(celltypes), ncol = length(recs),
746	                    dimnames = list(celltypes, recs))
747	  for (ct in celltypes) {
748	    tmp <- ccc_table %>% dplyr::filter(Receiver == ct) %>% dplyr::select(Receptor) %>% unique()
749	    Rmatrix[ct, tmp$Receptor] <- 1
750	  }
751	  
752	  ## Output files
753	  cat("Exporting input files for RaCiNG...\n")
754	  if (!dir.exists(output_folder)) dir.create(output_folder, recursive = TRUE)
755	  utils::write.csv(Lmatrix, file.path(output_folder, paste0("Lmatrix_", file_name, ".csv")))
756	  utils::write.csv(Rmatrix, file.path(output_folder, paste0("Rmatrix_", file_name, ".csv")))
757	  utils::write.csv(deconv, file.path(output_folder, paste0("Cmatrix_", file_name, ".csv")))
758	  utils::write.csv(LR_matrix, file.path(output_folder, paste0("LRmatrix_", file_name, ".csv")))
759	  utils::write.csv(ccc_table, file.path(output_folder, paste0("CC_table_", file_name, ".csv")), row.names = FALSE)
760	  
761	  cat("Input files generated and saved to:", output_folder, "\n")
762	
763	  ## Read the written CSVs back through generateInput to obtain the
764	
765	  ## normalised matrices and 3-D tensor expected by downstream functions.
766	  cat("Processing input matrices...\n")
767	  processed <- generateInput(file_name, output_folder = output_folder,
768	                             read_signs = signed)
769	
770	  ## Append the CC table to the processed result
771	  processed$CC_table <- ccc_table
772	
773	  return(processed)
774	}
